manifest.note: Objects that fit no other dataset. Each has a SIMBAD position and a distance from a cited paper abstract (retrieved via arxiv.org/abs pages and SIMBAD TAP at https://simbad.cfa.harvard.edu/simbad/sim-tap/sync). Distances are published estimates with the paper's method (geometric / VLBI parallax / expansion geometry), uncertainties as published (asymmetric ones store the larger side, the text of each fact has both). Positions are SIMBAD epoch-2000 ICRS coordinates; moving objects (pulsars, Cyg X-1) are not propagated. Considered and dropped: none of the six candidates; no other candidate was examined. Candidates were Sagittarius A*, Cygnus X-1, Crab Pulsar, SN 1987A, Eta Carinae, Vela Pulsar. Eta Carinae's distance is contested (see its facts). SIMBAD terms and CDS acknowledgement text were not retrieved (cds.unistra.fr licence page returned 404).

source.label: Abuter, R. et al. (2019), "A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty", arXiv:1904.05721, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201935656

coordinateSource.label: SIMBAD main object "NAME Sgr A*"; SIMBAD ICRS position (epoch 2000 coordinate as given by SIMBAD), coordinate reference 2011AJ....142...35P, wavelength R, major error axis 2.65 mas

facts.text: The distance from the Sun to the Galactic Center, R0, is 8178 pc with a statistical uncertainty of 13 pc and a systematic uncertainty of 22 pc, a geometric estimate from the orbit of the star S2 around Sgr A*.

references.label: Abuter, R. et al. (2019), "A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty", arXiv:1904.05721, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201935656

facts.text: S2 follows a 16-year orbit around the massive black hole Sgr A*; it was followed astrometrically and spectroscopically for 27 years.

references.label: Abuter, R. et al. (2019), "A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty", arXiv:1904.05721, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201935656

facts.text: S2 passed the pericenter of its highly eccentric orbit in May 2018, and the passage was followed with dense sampling throughout the year.

references.label: Abuter, R. et al. (2019), "A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty", arXiv:1904.05721, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201935656

facts.text: The gravitational redshift term in the S2 data is detected at a significance level of 20 sigma, with f_redshift = 1.04 +- 0.05.

references.label: Abuter, R. et al. (2019), "A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty", arXiv:1904.05721, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201935656

facts.text: SIMBAD's main identifier for this object is "NAME Sgr A*" and its main object type is X (X-ray Source).

source.label: Miller-Jones, James C. A. et al. (2021), "Cygnus X-1 contains a 21-solar mass black hole -- implications for massive star winds", arXiv:2102.09091, doi:10.1126/science.abb3363

facts.text: Radio astrometry gives a distance to the black hole X-ray binary Cygnus X-1 of 2.22 (+0.18, -0.17) kiloparsecs.

facts.text: Combined with previous optical data, this distance implies a black hole mass of 21.2 +- 2.2 solar masses, higher than previous measurements.

references.label: Miller-Jones, James C. A. et al. (2021), "Cygnus X-1 contains a 21-solar mass black hole -- implications for massive star winds", arXiv:2102.09091, doi:10.1126/science.abb3363

source.label: Lin, Rebecca et al. (2023), "The Radio Parallax of the Crab Pulsar: A First VLBI Measurement Calibrated with Giant Pulses", arXiv:2306.01617, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/acdc98

coordinateSource.label: SIMBAD main object "V* CM Tau"; SIMBAD ICRS position (epoch 2000 coordinate as given by SIMBAD), coordinate reference 2020yCat.1350....0G, wavelength O, major error axis 0.0732 mas

facts.text: A VLBI radio parallax of the Crab Pulsar, 0.53 +- 0.06 mas, yields a distance of 1.90 (+0.22, -0.18) kpc.

references.label: Lin, Rebecca et al. (2023), "The Radio Parallax of the Crab Pulsar: A First VLBI Measurement Calibrated with Giant Pulses", arXiv:2306.01617, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/acdc98

facts.text: Its proper motion is (-11.34 +- 0.06, 2.65 +- 0.14) mas/yr in (RA, Dec), giving a transverse velocity of 104 (+13, -11) km/s.

references.label: Lin, Rebecca et al. (2023), "The Radio Parallax of the Crab Pulsar: A First VLBI Measurement Calibrated with Giant Pulses", arXiv:2306.01617, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/acdc98

facts.text: The radio parallax and proper motion are consistent with the Gaia 3 measurements.

references.label: Lin, Rebecca et al. (2023), "The Radio Parallax of the Crab Pulsar: A First VLBI Measurement Calibrated with Giant Pulses", arXiv:2306.01617, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/acdc98

coordinateSource.label: SIMBAD main object "SN 1987A"; SIMBAD ICRS position (epoch 2000 coordinate as given by SIMBAD), coordinate reference 2025A&A...704A.272T, wavelength O, major error axis 16.3 mas

facts.text: From the absolute size of the circumstellar ring, R = (6.23 +/- 0.08)e17 cm, and its angular size, 808 +/- 17 mas, the distance to SN 1987A is 51.4 +/- 1.2 kpc (distance modulus 18.55 +/- 0.05).

references.label: Panagia, Nino (2003), "A Geometric Determination of the Distance to SN 1987A and the LMC", arXiv:astro-ph/0309416

facts.text: Allowing for the displacement of SN 1987A from the LMC centre, the distance to the barycenter of the Large Magellanic Cloud is estimated as 51.7 +/- 1.3 kpc.

references.label: Panagia, Nino (2003), "A Geometric Determination of the Distance to SN 1987A and the LMC", arXiv:astro-ph/0309416

objects.name: Eta Carinae
objects.classification: Massive star surrounded by the Homunculus nebula

source.label: Smith, Nathan (2006), "The Structure of the Homunculus: I. Shape and Latitude Dependence from H2 and [Fe II] Velocity Maps of Eta Carinae", arXiv:astro-ph/0602464, doi:10.1086/503766

coordinateSource.label: SIMBAD main object "* eta Car"; SIMBAD ICRS position (epoch 2000 coordinate as given by SIMBAD), coordinate reference 2012yCat.1322....0Z, wavelength O, major error axis 20.0 mas

facts.text: Near-infrared long-slit spectra of the Homunculus nebula resolve it into a thin outer shell seen in H2 and a warmer, thicker inner layer seen in [Fe II]; the H2 emission yields the shape of the nebula, a distance of 2350 +- 50 pc and an inclination angle of 41 degrees.

references.label: Smith, Nathan (2006), "The Structure of the Homunculus: I. Shape and Latitude Dependence from H2 and [Fe II] Velocity Maps of Eta Carinae", arXiv:astro-ph/0602464, doi:10.1086/503766

facts.text: Gaia parallaxes for the star cluster Trumpler 16 reveal a discrepancy in the oft-quoted distance of Eta Carinae; the authors state it is probably more distant and more luminous.

references.label: Davidson, Kris et al. (2018), "Gaia, Trumpler 16, and Eta Carinae", arXiv:1808.02073

facts.text: SIMBAD's main identifier for this object is "* eta Car" and its main object type is s*b (Blue Supergiant).

source.label: Dodson, R. et al. (2003), "The Vela Pulsar's proper motion and parallax derived from VLBI observations", arXiv:astro-ph/0302374, doi:10.1086/378089

coordinateSource.label: SIMBAD main object "NAME Vela Pulsar"; SIMBAD ICRS position (epoch 2000 coordinate as given by SIMBAD), coordinate reference 2004AJ....127.3587F, wavelength R, major error axis 11.37 mas

facts.text: VLBI observations at 2.3 and 8.4 GHz over 6.8 years (eleven epochs) give a parallax for the Vela pulsar of 3.4 +- 0.2 mas, equivalent to a distance of 293 (+19, -17) pc.

references.label: Dodson, R. et al. (2003), "The Vela Pulsar's proper motion and parallax derived from VLBI observations", arXiv:astro-ph/0302374, doi:10.1086/378089

facts.text: Its proper motion is -49.61 +- 0.06 mas/yr in RA (times cos dec) and 29.8 +- 0.1 mas/yr in Dec.

references.label: Dodson, R. et al. (2003), "The Vela Pulsar's proper motion and parallax derived from VLBI observations", arXiv:astro-ph/0302374, doi:10.1086/378089

facts.text: The Vela pulsar is the brightest pulsar at radio wavelengths.

references.label: Dodson, R. et al. (2003), "The Vela Pulsar's proper motion and parallax derived from VLBI observations", arXiv:astro-ph/0302374, doi:10.1086/378089
